# Decision: where the ATOMICS UI runs when agents live in a VM on Apple Silicon (spike v1)

Status: measured 2026-11-02 on throwaway VMs, all since removed. Recommendation: **path C**, the native macOS
client with agents, the chief and SQL Server in one Apple Virtualization (VZ) + Rosetta VM. Path B also works
and holds 60 fps, but it is capped at 60 Hz, adds two GPU translation stacks and a second hypervisor to the UI
path, and leads away from the daemon design. No ATOMICS code changed; the measurement patch below was applied
to a scratch copy only.

**Built (v5).** Path C is now generated by the flake (`programs.atomics.macDesktop`; see
[the NixOS VM setup](../nixos-vm.md)). Measured again with the same scene, every tile running in the VM
through the generated wrapper: 119–120 fps at 120 Hz on the built-in display, keystroke echo in a frame
7.7 ms p50 / 9.2 ms p95, wrapper PTY round trip 0.51 ms p50 (summarised in
[the NixOS VM setup](../nixos-vm.md#measured)). Building it changed three things this record
assumed: Lima's plain mode drops mounts, so the guest leaves plain mode and runs Lima's guest agent;
Lima's virtiofs tags are hashes, read from cidata; and Codex hooks get their pane from
`ATOMICS_HOOK_PANE`, since their command must stay identical across panes and ancestry stops at ssh.

Part of the plan for ATOMICS with its agents in a NixOS VM on Apple Silicon (Docker with Rosetta for amd64
containers such as SQL Server, warm .NET caches, a GPU-accelerated UI with no software rendering).

## The two paths

- **B.** ATOMICS, its agents and the chief in a UTM QEMU (HVF) VM with virtio-gpu (Venus for Vulkan, virgl
  for GL). SQL Server in a second, small VZ + Rosetta VM holding only Docker. Testcontainers in the UI VM uses
  `DOCKER_HOST` to it, and a systemd port forward makes `127.0.0.1:11433` in the UI VM reach the SQL container
  (the test suite in use expected that address).
- **C.** ATOMICS native on macOS (Metal). Agents and the chief in one VZ + Rosetta VM over SSH (the
  `[[agents]]` command is an ssh wrapper). Hooks and MCP reach the ATOMICS socket through an ssh-forwarded
  unix socket. Worktrees are shared at identical paths over virtiofs. SQL Server runs in Docker in that VM.

Rosetta for Linux exists only under VZ, and VZ gives Linux guests no GPU. SQL Server segfaults under
qemu-user. So a GPU-accelerated Linux UI (B) needs a second VM for SQL Server, and a Rosetta VM (C) needs
the UI outside it.

## Results

| | **B: UTM QEMU + Venus** | **C: native macOS** |
| --- | --- | --- |

| Other adapters offered | llvmpipe (Vulkan, Cpu), virgl (GL) | none |
| Rendered size | 2560×1440 (whole guest output) | 2560×1378 (maximized window; menu and title bars take the rest of 1440) |

| Frame interval p50 / p95 / p99 | 16.6 / 18.7–19.5 / 19.5–20.7 ms | 16.7 / 16.9–17.0 / 17.0–17.2 ms |
| Frames over 20 ms / over 34 ms, per 5 s | 1–9 / 0 | 0–2 / 0 |
| Frames reaching the Mac's display process | 59.8–60.0/s, p99 19–21 ms, none over 34 ms (UTM's renderer log) | not applicable (native) |
| Capacity without vsync | not measurable: still 60 fps (Wayland frame callbacks, UTM's fixed 60 Hz guest refresh) | 199–240 fps, frame p50 3.7–4.3 ms |

| amd64 SQL Server 2022 ready | works, through the second VM and host forwards | 4.9–5.7 s for a fresh container, 4.6 s on restart |
| Testcontainers SQL Server (random port, then 11433) | 10.8 s, 6.0 s; both queries pass | 10.1 s, 5.8 s; both queries pass |
| `dotnet build`, Jellyfin (42 projects), on the agents' filesystem | not measured (scoped out) | 22.1 s cold, 17–18 s rebuild, 3.4–4.7 s after a one-line edit, on virtiofs (VM ext4: 19.5, 15–16, 2.3–2.4 s); see [.NET build](#net-build) |

Steady-state rows are the 5-second windows from 15 s to 40 s into each run. The first 10 s include startup
and session launch, and the last window includes the exit screenshot.

### The machine and the scene

- MacBook Pro (Mac17,7), M5 Max (18 cores: 6 super, 12 performance), 64 GB, macOS 26.5, driving a 2560×1440
  ROG PG278QR at 60 Hz (a 144/165 Hz panel set to 60 Hz), 1 point per pixel. The machine was shared with
  other agents during the runs.
- C's VM: Lima 2.2.0, VZ, Rosetta with binfmt (`flags: OCF`), 14 vCPU, 24 GiB, Ubuntu 26.04 (kernel 7.0),
  Docker 29.1.3, .NET SDK 10.0.114, virtiofs mount of the work folder at its identical path.
- B's UI VM: UTM 5.0.8 (notarized, run from a scratch folder), QEMU with HVF, `-device
  virtio-gpu-gl-pci,hostmem=8G,blob=true,venus=true`, SPICE `gl=es` (ANGLE on Metal; MoltenVK for Venus),
  8 vCPU, 16 GiB, Ubuntu 26.04, Mesa 26.0.8, sway 1.11 (wlroots GLES2 renderer on virgl) with a custom
  2560×1440@60 output and ATOMICS full screen. B's SQL VM: Lima, VZ + Rosetta, 4 vCPU, 6 GiB, Docker only.
- The same ATOMICS commit (`6b7efaf`) built for both, release profile, with a measurement patch in a scratch copy:
  - adapter info from `CreationContext::wgpu_render_state`;
  - frame intervals and `cpu_usage` in 5 s windows;
  - an optional repaint every frame and `AutoNoVsync`;
  - injected wheel scrolling over the diff (30 points per frame, reversing every 240 frames);
  - a probe that writes a marker into one terminal every 500 ms and times until `screen_text` shows the echo.

  Runs used isolated `ATOMICS_HOME`, `ATOMICS_SOCKET` and `ATOMICS_CONFIG` and went through
  `atomics queue --class qa`.
- Scene, identical in both: 8 tiles each streaming 200 coloured lines/s (`scroll.pl`), one echo tile, and the
  diff panel open on a 70-file diff (+11,478 −11,478 lines) of ATOMICS's own sources; `[layout]` set so all
  9 tiles and the diff are on screen at once. In C the tiles' programs ran in the VM through the ssh wrapper,
  in B locally in the UI VM.

## Path C in detail

**UI.** Native Metal holds vsync with no drops while the diff scrolls continuously and 8 tiles stream, and
without vsync it renders 4× faster than 60 Hz. With no injected scrolling, ATOMICS repaints at 21–28 fps,
driven by terminal output coalescing (100/200 ms per tile), as designed.

**Input latency.** The terminal tile's keystroke goes to a PTY running `ssh -tt <vm> …`. PTY echo round trips,
measured outside the app with a byte written and its echo read back (300 samples each):

| Path | p50 | p90 | p99 |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| local `cat` on the Mac | 0.05 ms | 0.06 ms | 0.09 ms |
| ssh into the VM, OpenSSH 10.2 defaults | 20.4 ms | 22.3 ms | 22.8 ms |
| ssh into the VM, `ObscureKeystrokeTiming=no` | 0.65–0.68 ms | 0.83–0.85 ms | 1.0–1.2 ms |
| same, with 8 tiles streaming through ssh at once | 0.59 ms | 0.77 ms | 0.96 ms |

OpenSSH 9.5 and later sends keystrokes on a 20 ms clock with chaff to hide typing rhythm. That one default
cost a frame or more per keystroke: in the app, keystroke-to-echo was 15.9 ms p50 and 33.1 ms p95 with it,
and 5.2 / 16.4 ms without (local: 4.7 / 12.3 ms). The rest is the app's frame cadence, the same as local.
Lima's port forwarder and VZ NAT behaved the same. **The agent wrapper must pass
`-o ObscureKeystrokeTiming=no`**, and on any ControlMaster it reuses, since a multiplexed session inherits
the master's setting. Present and display add the same 1–2 refreshes as any native app; they were not measured
(no Screen Recording permission was available for a camera-free end-to-end probe).

**SQL Server.** `mcr.microsoft.com/mssql/server:2022-latest` (16.0.4305.5, X64) with
`--platform linux/amd64` in the VM's Docker. `/proc/1/maps` in the container shows the Rosetta runtime.
"SQL Server is now ready for client connections" came 5.7, 4.9 and 5.2 s after `docker run` for three fresh
containers, and 4.6 s after restarting one. `sqlcmd` created a table and summed it. The image pull took 149 s.
Agents run in this VM, so `127.0.0.1:11433` is the container's published port: no forward is needed. The
Testcontainers check (a .NET 10 console app with `Testcontainers.MsSql`) started a random-port container in
10.1 s, including Ryuk, and a fixed `11433:1433` one in 5.8 s, and queried both.

**Hooks, MCP and ctl.** `ssh -R <sock>:<sock>` forwarded an isolated instance's `ATOMICS_SOCKET` into the VM at
the same path. The Linux `atomics ctl '{"cmd":"list"}'` returned the Mac instance's sessions: 6.0 ms per call
from the VM against 5.7 ms locally, both mostly process start. `atomics hook --pane <id>` ran without error
over the same socket. It exits 0 even when it cannot connect, so ctl is the proof that the socket works.
Three findings:

- Identical paths mean `/Users/<user>` must exist in the VM. The forward failed until it did. The VM user's
  home, or at least `/Users/<user>`, belongs at the Mac's path.
- ATOMICS writes hook commands with `setup::executable_path()`, the Mac binary's absolute path inside
  `ATOMICS.app`. In the VM that path needs a Linux `atomics` (a Nix-installed copy or symlink at the
  identical path), or hooks silently do nothing.
- Hooks route by `--pane`. Routing by process ancestry, used for SessionStart without a pane, cannot work
  across the boundary: the Mac sees only the `ssh` PID.

<a id="net-build"></a>
**.NET build.** Jellyfin at `7ab1c6bb` (2026-03-10): 42 projects, 1,962 `.cs` files, `net10.0`. This is
the newest commit whose own analyzer builds with the Ubuntu SDK's Roslyn 5.0; later commits need SDK 10.0.2xx.
Built inside the VM with 14 vCPU, Debug, after a warm restore; times in seconds.

| Step | virtiofs (Mac APFS worktree) | VM-local ext4 | virtiofs / ext4 |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| `dotnet restore`, packages already in the VM's NuGet cache | 2.4 | 1.6 | 1.5× |
| `dotnet build` after `git clean -xdf` and restore | 22.1 | 19.5 | 1.13× |
| `dotnet build --no-incremental`, twice | 18.1, 17.1 | 15.5, 14.9 | 1.16× |
| `dotnet build` with nothing changed | 2.3 | 1.5 | 1.5× |
| `dotnet build` after a one-line edit in `MediaBrowser.Model`, three times | 4.7, 4.0, 3.4 | 2.4, 2.3, 2.4 | about 1.7× |

Both builds finished with 244 warnings and 0 errors. The NuGet cache is on the VM's own disk in both
columns. Builds ran through `atomics queue --class test` while other agents shared the machine.

Full builds cost about 15% more on virtiofs, where compile time dominates. Small incremental builds, where
MSBuild's file checks dominate, cost 1.5–1.7×, about 1–2 s per build.

The virtiofs column is what agents use in C: worktrees live on the Mac's APFS and the VM sees them over
virtiofs. The ext4 column is the same tree on the VM's own disk, which is where worktrees live once the host
moves into the VM (see the mapping below). B's agents would use their VM's own disk (QEMU virtio-blk), which
was not measured.

**Setup.** One VZ VM, which Lima, vfkit or a NixOS module can describe declaratively. On the Mac:
- the existing `ATOMICS.app`;
- per agent, an ssh wrapper in `[[agents]] command` that `cd`s to the identical path;
- one long-lived reverse forward of the socket;
- a virtiofs share of the worktree root.

The VM was ready, with Docker, .NET and build tools installed, 5 min 19 s after `limactl start`.

**What the boundary protects.** Agent and chief processes, their logins and their builds run only in the VM.
The VM sees the shared worktree root (writable) and nothing else of the Mac. It reaches ATOMICS's socket,
which carries the full control API, exactly as a bare agent does today. ATOMICS runs git on the Mac in
worktrees the VM writes. That is the case `docs/isolation.md` handles for sandboxes, so git pinning and the
ref guard should cover VM worktrees too. The Mac keychain, the credential relay and other repositories stay
out of reach unless forwarded.

## Path B in detail

**UI.** Venus works: wgpu chose the Venus adapter over llvmpipe and virgl, rendered the scene correctly at
2560×1440, and held 60 fps. UTM's debug log records each guest frame its Metal renderer receives
(`cs_gl_draw`), and that host-side rate was also 60/s with a p99 of 19–21 ms. B is smooth at 60 Hz, but:

- **It cannot go above 60 Hz.** With vsync off and a repaint every frame it stayed at 60 fps. UTM 5.0.8 still
  gives guests a fixed 60 Hz. Its 5.0.7 notes planned to follow the host's refresh rate instead, a change
  described as also fixing Windows 3D acceleration on displays faster than 125 Hz, but dropped it from that
  release. Whether Linux guests are affected above 125 Hz was not tested. This display can run at 144 or
  165 Hz.
- Frame-to-frame jitter is higher than native (p99 about 20 ms against 17 ms), with a few frames over 20 ms in
  every window.
- The path crosses two translation stacks: wgpu → Venus → virglrenderer → MoltenVK → Metal for the app, and
  sway → virgl → ANGLE → Metal for the compositor. UTM's release notes say Vulkan-based Linux desktops do not
  render (no indirect draws for geometry shaders), so the compositor must stay on virgl GL.
- Input and display latency were not measured end to end. The spike scoped B to frame rate and SQL, and no Screen
  Recording or Accessibility permission was available. Every keystroke also crosses SPICE, virtio-input, the
  guest compositor and UTM's vblank-synced blit.

**SQL Server.** It works, but not as drawn. UTM's QEMU VM (vmnet shared, `192.168.65.0/24` on `bridge101`)
cannot reach a VZ NAT VM (`192.168.64.0/24` on `bridge100`): ping and TCP both failed. Lima documents vzNAT
as unreachable from other guests. What worked: Lima port forwards from the SQL VM bound to the Mac's
`bridge101` address, for Docker's TCP API on 2375 and every port from 1024 to 65535. Testcontainers in the UI
VM, with `DOCKER_HOST=tcp://192.168.65.1:2375`, started SQL Server on a random port in 10.8 s (Ryuk
included) and queried it at `192.168.65.1:32769` in 108 ms. A fixed-port container came up in 6.0 s, and
`127.0.0.1:11433` in the UI VM, through a `systemd-socket-proxyd` socket unit, answered in 40 ms. Without
forwarding every high port, Testcontainers' random ports and Ryuk do not work. The alternative is shared vmnet
networking, which needs root-installed `socket_vmnet` or both VMs under one manager that supports it.

**Setup.** UTM is a GUI app. A VM is a `config.plist` in a `.utm` bundle, and GPU behaviour comes from
UTM's global preferences (renderer backend, Vulkan driver), not the VM file. Scripting needs AppleScript
(an Automation consent prompt) or its URL scheme. Here the bundle was written by hand, the disk grown by
editing the qcow2 header (UTM ships no `qemu-img`), and the guest seeded with cloud-init. Add a second VM
manager for the SQL VM, the host-side forwards and the UI VM's socket unit.

**What the boundary protects.** Everything, UI included, is in the UI VM, so ATOMICS itself is contained too.
The cost is attack surface on the Mac: guest-controlled GPU command streams decoded by virglrenderer, Venus,
MoltenVK and ANGLE inside UTM's QEMU process. Docker's unauthenticated TCP API is also reachable from
anything on `bridge101`, which means root in the SQL VM.

## Recommendation

**Take C.** It meets the hard requirement with margin: native Metal at a steady 60 fps, about 4× headroom
for 120–165 Hz, and no translation layers. Its seams cost nothing measurable once the wrapper disables ssh
keystroke obfuscation (0.6 ms echo round trip). SQL Server runs next to the agents with no networking glue.
It is also the shape `docs/daemon.md` already plans: a native client on the Mac, the runtime and agents in the
VM.

Trade-offs accepted with C:

- Builds read and write worktrees over virtiofs until the host moves into the VM: about 15% slower full
  builds and 1.5–1.7× slower small incremental ones (1–2 s each) than VM-local ext4.
- Identical paths: the VM needs `/Users/<user>`, and a Linux `atomics` at the Mac binary's path for hooks.
- An ATOMICS quit or restart closes the ssh PTYs and stops the agents in the VM, as quitting does today.
  Claude sessions resume. Keeping agents alive across client restarts is daemon phase 3's job, not C's.
- The UI is outside the VM, so the VM boundary does not contain ATOMICS itself. What it holds back are the
  agents, which is the point of the VM.

B remains a fallback only if the UI must be inside the VM. It would need a 60 Hz display mode, the virgl
compositor, and shared VM networking for SQL.

## How C maps onto docs/daemon.md

C as spiked is daemon.md's destination with the host still on the Mac. The daemon's phase 3 runs the host
headless and talks to clients over a versioned WebSocket protocol. Put that host in the VM and C's
seams disappear:

| Piece | C today | Host in the VM, client on the Mac |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Agent launch | Host on the Mac spawns `ssh -tt vm 'cd <same path> && exec claude …'` in a Mac PTY | Host in the VM spawns `claude` in a VM PTY; the wrapper is gone |
| PTY and emulator | On the Mac; bytes cross ssh | In the VM (daemon: "the host owns the PTY"); screen snapshots and deltas cross to the client |
| Hooks and MCP | Linux `atomics hook`/`mcp` in the VM → ssh-forwarded unix socket → Mac host | Same commands, local socket in the VM (daemon: "do not publish it through ingress") |
| Chief's `atomics ctl` | Through the forwarded socket | Local socket |
| Worktrees and git | APFS on the Mac, virtiofs into the VM at identical paths | VM-local disk; diffs and file content go to the client over the protocol ("paths are host paths") |
| Builds, Docker, SQL | In the VM | In the VM (unchanged) |
| Mac ↔ VM channel | One ssh connection per agent plus one reverse forward | One authenticated WebSocket (phase 3 pairing) over a forwarded port or vsock |
| Credentials and relay | Mac keychain and loopback relay; VM agents would need a forward | Daemon's headless credentials in the VM ("do not rely on a desktop keychain") |

To keep that move easy, C should avoid:

- **Teaching the runtime about the VM.** Keep the boundary in configuration: the `[[agents]]` wrapper command,
  the env it passes and the socket forward. No "remote session" kind, path translation, per-host binary
  rewriting or VM fields in `sessions.json`. Those would have to be unwound when the host moves.
- **Depending on Mac PIDs for agents.** Route hooks by `--pane` (pass `ATOMICS_PANE` through the wrapper's
  remote command), and don't add liveness checks, signals or resource sampling keyed on the PTY child's PID.
  In C that PID is `ssh`. In the end state it is local again.
- **Building persistence in C.** tmux or dtach in the VM to survive client restarts duplicates phase 3,
  where the host keeps PTYs while clients come and go.
- **New client features that read worktrees directly.** The native client reads APFS today; in the end state
  it gets content only over the protocol. New panels should go through the host's diff and file APIs
  (`diff_get`, `file_get`), not the filesystem.
- **Mac-only filesystem tricks for worktrees.** Warm templates and copies that rely on APFS clones won't
  exist on ext4 in the VM (no reflink); keep them behind the host and filesystem-agnostic.
- **Widening the forwarded socket.** It carries the full control API. Keep the restricted
  `atomics mcp --agent` surface separate from the chief's, as now. Don't expose the socket over TCP to make
  forwarding easier. In the end state it is local to the VM.
- **Tying credentials to the Mac.** Give the VM's agents and chief their logins in the VM (`az`, MCP sign-in),
  as the plan already says, rather than forwarding the Mac relay into the VM. The relay then moves with the host.
- **Forgetting the ssh lesson in the protocol.** Keystrokes in phase 3 cross a WebSocket. Send them
  immediately (`TCP_NODELAY`, no batching or obfuscation) and repeat the echo measurement above against it.

## Not measured, and why

- **B's input latency and build time.** The spike scoped B to frame rate on its GPU adapter and whether SQL works.
- **End-to-end keystroke-to-photon latency on either path.** That needs screen capture or event injection,
  and this session had neither Screen Recording nor Accessibility permission. In-app and PTY-level numbers
  stand in for it, and C's display path is the same as any native app's.
- **The UI above 60 Hz.** The monitor ran at 60 Hz, and changing the user's display settings was out of scope.
  C's no-vsync capacity (199–240 fps) and UTM's fixed 60 Hz guest refresh decide the question anyway.
- **A macOS-native build baseline.** Building downloaded third-party code on the Mac was not allowed, so
  Jellyfin was built only inside the throwaway VM.

## Cleanup

Removed after the spike:
- both Lima VMs and their Lima home;
- the UTM VM bundle, `UTM.app` (never installed in `/Applications`, unregistered from LaunchServices) and
  UTM's container data;
- the Ubuntu cloud image, `UTM.dmg`, the Jellyfin clone and its NuGet packages;
- the build outputs, the isolated ATOMICS home and the throwaway SSH keys.

macOS refuses to let a shell delete the two now-empty container folders
`~/Library/Containers/com.utmapp.UTM` and `com.utmapp.QEMUHelper` (76 KB of `containermanagerd`
metadata). They can be moved to the Trash in Finder. The machine's other Lima VMs, Docker Desktop and
NuGet cache were not touched.
